```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3)
library(powerscope)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

## What the package computes

Every design is reduced to a true effect *D* and the standard error *SE* of
its estimate. One engine, `ps_retrodesign()`, then returns:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `power` | P(result is significant) |
| `type_s` | P(estimate has the wrong sign \| significant) |
| `exaggeration` | E(\|estimate\| \| significant) / \|D\| (Type M) |
| `min_sig_ratio` | smallest overestimation any significant result can have |

Power alone does not describe what a significant result from a weak design
means. At low power, significant estimates are large overestimates and can
have the wrong sign (Gelman & Carlin 2014). The Gelman, Hill & Vehtari (2020)
Figure 16.1 design, true effect 2 with SE 8.1:

```{r}
ps_retrodesign(effect = 2, se = 8.1)
```

All inputs that describe biology (effect sizes, SDs, dispersions, allele
frequencies, overdispersion, fraction of true effects) must come from your
own pilot data, prior studies or the literature. The package has no defaults
for them.

## Means and proportions

`ps_means()` is exact for the t-test on normal data, including the
exaggeration ratio. `ps_props()` enumerates all binomial outcomes when that is
feasible, so it is exact for the z-test actually run.

```{r, eval = has_gg}
r <- ps_means(delta = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.8), sd = 1, n1 = 3:60)
ps_plot(r, "n1", group = "delta", target_power = 0.8)
```

```{r}
ps_sample_size(ps_means, "n1", target_power = 0.8, delta = 0.5, sd = 1, link = list(n2 = 1))
ps_props(p1 = 0.1, p2 = 0.2, n1 = 100, n2 = 150)
```

## RNA-seq differential expression

Single gene, negative binomial with dispersion φ (Hart et al. 2013):

```{r, eval = has_gg}
r <- ps_rnaseq(log2fc = 1, mean_count = c(10, 50, 500), dispersion = 0.1, n1 = 2:15)
ps_plot(r, "n1", group = "mean_count", target_power = 0.8)
```

Across all genes, using means and dispersions estimated from your own data,
with the per-gene level that gives BH FDR *q* (Jung 2005):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(DESeq2)
dds <- DESeq(dds)   # pilot or previous experiment, same tissue/platform
genes <- data.frame(gene_id = rownames(dds),
                    mean_count = mcols(dds)$baseMean,
                    dispersion = mcols(dds)$dispersion)
res <- ps_rnaseq_genes(genes, log2fc = 1, n1 = 4, q = 0.05, pi1 = 0.1)
res$summary
```

```{r}
set.seed(1)   # simulated table for illustration only
genes <- data.frame(mean_count = rlnorm(3000, log(100), 1.5),
                    dispersion = rlnorm(3000, log(0.1), 0.6))
sapply(3:8, function(n)
  ps_rnaseq_genes(genes, log2fc = 1, n1 = n, q = 0.05, pi1 = 0.1)$summary$mean_power)
```

`exaggeration_among_discoveries` in the summary is the expected inflation of
the raw fold change among DE genes that reach significance. This is why
shrunken estimates (e.g. `DESeq2::lfcShrink`) should be reported for ranked
gene lists.

## Pooled sequencing

Two-stage binomial sampling: chromosomes into the pool, then reads from the
pool. `overdispersion` (≥ 1) inflates the variance for unequal individual
contributions and library effects; estimate it from replicate pools.

```{r, eval = has_gg}
r <- ps_poolseq(p1 = 0.5, p2 = 0.6, pool_size1 = c(20, 50, 200), depth1 = seq(10, 300, 5))
ps_plot(r, "depth1", group = "pool_size1")
```

Read depth beyond the number of chromosomes in the pool adds little. The
`1/(ploidy * pool_size)` term sets a floor on the variance.

## Association

```{r}
ps_casecontrol(maf = 0.2, odds_ratio = 1.3, n_cases = c(1000, 3000, 5000), n_controls = 5000)
ps_mde(ps_qtl, "beta_sd", 0.8, maf = 0.25, n = 2000, interval = c(1e-3, 1))
```

The default `alpha = 5e-8` is the human genome-wide convention. For other
species or marker sets, derive the threshold from the effective number of
independent tests in your data.

## Checking an approximation by simulation

`ps_simulate()` runs the test a user would actually run, with estimated
nuisance parameters, and returns empirical power, Type S and exaggeration.

```{r}
p <- list(p1 = 0.2, p2 = 0.4, pool_size1 = 30, depth1 = 40, n_pools1 = 3)
do.call(ps_poolseq, p)[, .(power, type_s, exaggeration)]
ps_simulate("poolseq", p, n_sims = 2e4, seed = 1)
```

The full analytic-versus-simulation comparison for every design is produced
by `validation/run_validation.R` in the source repository.

## Assumptions

* Analytic results for RNA-seq, pool-seq and case-control use Wald tests with
  asymptotic normal estimates. With very few replicates, rare alleles or low
  counts, the test actually run can differ by a few percentage points of
  power; check with `ps_simulate()`.
* RNA-seq power assumes known dispersion. DESeq2/edgeR estimate and shrink it,
  so realised power with 2–3 replicates is lower.
* Pool-seq assumes equal contributions of individuals unless
  `overdispersion` is set.
* Association assumes Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, a multiplicative
  (case-control) or additive (QTL) model, and no population structure.
* A single assumed true effect is a model input. Report results over a range
  of plausible effects.
